children.name: Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines
children.blurb: Reproducible notebooks and pipelines cover the practices and tooling that let a quantitative analysis be rerun by someone else, or by the original author later, with the same data, code, environment and results.

children.name: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
children.blurb: Asking data questions in plain language covers systems that let analysts, researchers, and domain experts query structured datasets without writing SQL or code.

children.name: Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data
children.blurb: Large-scale compute on institutional data covers the use of distributed and high performance computing to analyze datasets held by universities, hospitals, government agencies and corporations.

children.blurb: Writing statistical code with AI covers using language models and code assistants to draft, debug, document, and translate statistical programs in languages such as R, Python, and Stan.

children.blurb: Testing a study design before data collection means checking whether a planned quantitative study can answer its research question before resources are spent gathering real data.

sections.body: This field is about making quantitative work with AI checkable and repeatable. Right now AI is being used to generate notebook cells that load data, clean missing values, and plot results, and to turn a plain English question into a database query or a statistical test. It is also being used to write code for regressions, simulations, and power calculations before a study begins. The work is practical: it produces scripts, notebooks, and test plans that a researcher can run, not just conceptual descriptions.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Reproducible notebooks and pipelines are now common, but AI-generated code still fails silently when a library version changes or a column name is misspelled. Asking data questions in plain language works well for simple counts and filters, but it breaks down when a question requires domain knowledge or a custom metric. Large-scale compute on institutional data is possible, yet access controls, data governance, and cost limits are often the real bottleneck, not model quality. Statistical code generation is reliable for textbook methods, but it can produce wrong degrees of freedom or ignore assumptions when a design is unusual. Testing a study design before data collection is promising, but the simulated data is only as good as the assumptions typed into the prompt.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader who wants to make a notebook that another person can rerun should start with Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines. If the goal is to query a dataset without writing SQL or Python, Asking Data Questions in Plain Language shows what works and where it fails. Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data covers the practical side of running jobs on sensitive or very large datasets. Writing Statistical Code with AI is the page for checking whether a generated t-test, mixed model, or bootstrap is trustworthy. Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection explains how to simulate data and run a pilot analysis before committing to a real experiment.
